results.title: Order polynomial of a subgroup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a subgroup $H$ of a group, the order polynomial of $H$ is $f(H) = \prod_p x_p^{v_p(|H|)}$ in the integer polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_0, x_1, \dots]$, where $p$ runs over the primes, $x_p$ is the variable indexed by $p$, and $v_p(|H|)$ is the exponent of $p$ in the order $|H|$ of $H$. If $H$ is infinite, $f(H) = 1$.

results.title: Eulerian function of a group (G. E. Wall)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a group and let $f$ be the order polynomial. A function $\varphi$ from the subgroups of $G$ to the integer polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_0, x_1, \dots]$ is an Eulerian function of $G$ if $\sum_{K \le H} \varphi(K) = f(H)$ for every subgroup $H$ of $G$, the sum running over the subgroups $K$ of $H$. The value $\varphi(G)$ is the Eulerian polynomial of $G$.

results.title: $p$-solvable group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $p$, a group $G$ is $p$-solvable if it has a chain of subgroups $1 = N_0 \le N_1 \le \dots \le N_n = G$ in which each $N_i$ is normal in $N_{i+1}$ and each index $[N_{i+1} : N_i]$, taken to be $0$ when it is infinite, is a power $p^k$ with $k \ge 0$ or is coprime to $p$. For finite $G$ and prime $p$ this says that every factor $N_{i+1}/N_i$ is a $p$-group or has order prime to $p$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 11.104(a) (Eulerian polynomials and solvability, G. E. Wall)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the statement that for every finite group $G$ and every Eulerian function $\varphi$ of $G$, with values in the integer polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_0, x_1, \dots]$: if there are a finite set $S$ of primes and, for each $q \in S$, an integer polynomial $P_q$ involving no variable other than $x_q$, such that the Eulerian polynomial $\varphi(G)$ equals $\prod_{q \in S} P_q$, then $G$ is solvable.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 11.104(b) (Eulerian polynomials and $p$-solvability)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the statement that for every finite group $G$, every prime $p$ and every Eulerian function $\varphi$ of $G$, with values in the integer polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_0, x_1, \dots]$: if the Eulerian polynomial $\varphi(G)$ is a product $PQ$ of integer polynomials where $P$ involves no variable other than $x_p$ and $x_p$ does not occur in $Q$, then $G$ is $p$-solvable.

results.title: Solvability from one-variable factorizations of the Eulerian polynomial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group and let $\varphi$ be an Eulerian function of $G$, with values in the integer polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_0, x_1, \dots]$. If there are a finite set $S$ of primes and, for each $q \in S$, an integer polynomial $P_q$ involving no variable other than $x_q$, such that the Eulerian polynomial $\varphi(G)$ equals $\prod_{q \in S} P_q$, then $G$ is solvable.

results.title: Eulerian polynomial factorization implies $p$-solvability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, let $p$ be a prime, and let $\varphi$ be an Eulerian function of $G$, with values in the integer polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_0, x_1, \dots]$. If the Eulerian polynomial $\varphi(G)$ is a product $PQ$ of integer polynomials where $P$ involves no variable other than $x_p$ and $x_p$ does not occur in $Q$, then $G$ is $p$-solvable.

results.caption: Definition

results.title: A sequence supported at index zero has zero discrepancy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, let $v \in K$, let $q$ be a positive integer and let $a \in \mathbb{N}$. The sequence with value $v$ at index $0$ and $0$ at every other index has discrepancy $0$ at modulus $q$ and residue $a$.

results.title: Discrepancy of a single positive term
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, let $n$ be a positive integer, let $v \in K$, let $q$ be a positive integer and let $a \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $e$ be the sequence with value $v$ at index $n$ and $0$ at every other index. Then the discrepancy of $e$ at modulus $q$ and residue $a$ equals $A - B/\varphi(q)$, where $A = v$ if $n \equiv a \pmod{q}$ and $A = 0$ otherwise, $B = v$ if $\gcd(n, q) = 1$ and $B = 0$…

results.title: Primitive discrepancy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finitely supported sequence $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a positive integer $q$, the primitive discrepancy of $\alpha$ modulo $q$ is the maximum, over the residue classes $a$ modulo $q$ that are coprime to $q$, of $|\Delta(\alpha; a \bmod q)|$, where $\Delta(\alpha; a \bmod q)$ is the discrepancy of $\alpha$ in the residue class of $a$ modulo $q$.

results.title: The primitive discrepancy is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finitely supported sequence $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every positive integer $q$, there is a residue class $a$ modulo $q$ coprime to $q$ such that the primitive discrepancy of $\alpha$ modulo $q$ equals $|\Delta(\alpha; a \bmod q)|$, the absolute value of the discrepancy of $\alpha$ in the residue class of $a$ modulo $q$.

results.title: Primitive residue-class discrepancies are bounded by the primitive discrepancy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finitely supported real sequence indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, let $q$ be a positive integer, and let $a$ be a unit of $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$, represented by its least nonnegative residue. Then the absolute value of the discrepancy of $\alpha$ at modulus $q$ and residue $a$ is at most the primitive discrepancy of $\alpha$ at modulus $q$.

results.title: Averaged discrepancy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finitely supported real sequence $\alpha$ indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ and a natural number $Q$, the averaged discrepancy of $\alpha$ up to $Q$ is the sum $\sum_{q=1}^{Q} \Delta^*(\alpha; q)$, where $\Delta^*(\alpha; q)$ is the primitive discrepancy of $\alpha$ at modulus $q$.

results.title: The averaged discrepancy with cutoff zero vanishes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finitely supported real sequence $\alpha$ indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, the averaged discrepancy of $\alpha$ with cutoff $Q = 0$ equals $0$, since there are no positive moduli $q \le 0$.

results.title: Multiplicative convolution of finitely supported sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring and let $\alpha, \beta \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ be finitely supported. Their convolution $\alpha \star \beta$ is the finitely supported sequence whose value at $n$ is $\sum_{a, b \ge 1,\ ab = n} \alpha(a)\beta(b)$; the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ at index $0$ are discarded.

results.title: Coefficients of the multiplicative convolution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring and let $\alpha, \beta \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ be finitely supported, with convolution $\alpha \star \beta$. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

results.title: The multiplicative convolution vanishes at index zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring and let $\alpha, \beta \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ be finitely supported. Then their convolution $\alpha \star \beta$ has value $0$ at index $0$.

results.title: Convolving a sequence supported at zero gives zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring, let $v \in R$, and let $\beta \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ be finitely supported. If $e$ is the sequence with value $v$ at index $0$ and $0$ at every other index, then the convolution $e \star \beta$ is the zero sequence.

results.title: Convolving with a sequence supported at zero gives zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring, let $\alpha \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ be finitely supported, and let $v \in R$. If $e$ is the sequence with value $v$ at index $0$ and $0$ at every other index, then the convolution $\alpha \star e$ is the zero sequence.

results.title: Von Mangoldt function on a dyadic interval
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real number $x$, this is the finitely supported function on $\mathbb{N}$ whose value at $n$ is $\Lambda(n)$ when $n \ge 1$ and $x \le n \le 2x$, and $0$ otherwise, where $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt function.

results.title: Values of the dyadic von Mangoldt function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real $x > 0$ and every natural number $n$, the von Mangoldt function on the dyadic interval for $x$ takes at $n$ the value $\Lambda(n)$ if $x \le n \le 2x$, and $0$ otherwise, where $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt function.

results.title: Distance between lines
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For lines $x$ and $y$ through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ is $\sin \theta$, where $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ is the angle between nonzero vectors spanning $x$ and $y$. This is the usual distance on the projective space.

results.title: Distance from a line to a subspace
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a line $x$ through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a subspace $y$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ is the infimum, over all lines $y'$ contained in $y$, of the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x, y')$ between the lines $x$ and $y'$. When $y = 0$ there is no such line and the value is $0$.

results.title: Distance between subspaces
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For subspaces $x$ and $y$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ is defined as follows. If $\dim y \le \dim x$, it is the supremum, over all lines $y'$ contained in $y$, of the distance $\operatorname{dist}(y', x)$ from the line $y'$ to the subspace $x$. If $\dim y > \dim x$, it is the supremum, over all lines $x'$ contained in $x$, of the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x', y)$ from the line…

results.title: The integer lattice
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is the $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule of $\mathbb{R}^d$ spanned by the standard basis vectors, that is, the lattice of points with integer coordinates.

results.title: Integer points of a subspace
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, this is the set $V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of integer points of $V$, as a $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule of $V$.

results.title: Rational subspace
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is rational if $V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ is a full-rank lattice in $V$, that is, a discrete subgroup of $V$ that spans $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$.

results.title: Chosen basis of a rational subspace
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a rational subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, this is a fixed choice of a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of the lattice $V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$, indexed by $\{0, \dots, \dim V - 1\}$ and viewed as an $\mathbb{R}$-basis of $V$.

results.title: Height of a rational subspace
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a rational subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ of dimension $k$, let $v_1, \dots, v_k$ be the chosen basis of the lattice $V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$. The height of $V$ is $H(V) = \lVert v_1 \wedge \dots \wedge v_k \rVert$, where the exterior power $\bigwedge^k \mathbb{R}^d$ carries the inner product whose value on decomposable elements $u_1 \wedge \dots \wedge u_k$ and $w_1 \wedge \dots \wedge w_k$ is the Gram…

results.summary: Let $x$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and let $k$ be a natural number. For subspaces $v$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ write $\operatorname{dist}(v, x)$ for the distance between the subspaces $v$ and $x$, and for a rational subspace $v$ write $H(v)$ for its height. results.title: Full-dimensional sets in $\mathbb{Z}^d$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$ is full-dimensional when it is not contained in an affine hyperplane: for every real vector $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and every real number $c$, if $\sum_i a_i x_i = c$ for all $x \in A$, then $a = 0$.

results.title: Statement of Stanchescu's difference set bound
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that for every integer $d \ge 2$ there is a natural number $N$ such that every full-dimensional finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$ (one not contained in an affine hyperplane) with $|A| \ge N$ satisfies $|A - A| \ge \left(2d - 2 + \frac{1}{d - 1}\right)|A| - (2d^2 - 4d + 3)$, where $A - A = \{a - b : a, b \in A\}$ is the difference set of $A$.

results.title: Conlon–Lim theorem: Stanchescu's difference set bound holds
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every integer $d \ge 2$ there is a natural number $N$ such that every finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$ with $|A| \ge N$ that is not contained in an affine hyperplane (no nonzero real linear functional is constant on $A$) satisfies $|A - A| \ge \left(2d - 2 + \frac{1}{d - 1}\right)|A| - (2d^2 - 4d + 3)$, where $A - A = \{a - b : a, b \in A\}$ is the difference set of $A$.

results.title: Linear spaces (2-designs)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A family $A_1, \dots, A_t$ of subsets of $\{1, \dots, v\}$ is a $2$-design (also called a pairwise balanced design or a linear space) when every block $A_i$ has at least two points and every pair of distinct points of $\{1, \dots, v\}$ lies in exactly one block.

results.title: Erdős Problem 903: line counts just above a projective plane
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the statement that for every prime power $p$, with $n = p^2 + p + 1$, every $2$-design $A_1, \dots, A_t$ on $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with more than $n$ blocks has at least $n + p$ blocks. Here a $2$-design is a family of subsets in which every block has at least two points and every pair of distinct points lies in exactly one block.

results.title: Erdős–Fowler–Sós–Wilson gap above a projective plane (Erdős Problem 903)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime power and $n = p^2 + p + 1$. Let $A_1, \dots, A_t$ be a $2$-design on $\{1, \dots, n\}$: every block $A_i$ has at least two points and every pair of distinct points lies in exactly one block. If $t > n$, then $t \ge n + p$.

results.title: Number of marked letters

The number of marked letters of a marked word $w$ is the number of letters of $w$ that are marked, counted with multiplicity.

results.title: Alternating selection with a flag
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a flag $b$ (true or false) and a list $\ell$, the alternating selection of $\ell$ with initial flag $b$ is defined by recursion on $\ell$: the empty list gives the empty list; for a list with head $a$ and tail $\ell'$, if $b$ is true it keeps $a$ and continues on $\ell'$ with flag false, and if $b$ is false it drops $a$ and continues on $\ell'$ with flag true.

results.title: Sample of a catalog
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sample of a list $[x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots]$ is the list $[x_0, x_2, x_4, \dots]$ of every other element, starting with the first, in their original order.

results.title: Alternating selection gives a sublist
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every flag $b$ (true or false) and every list $\ell$, the alternating selection of $\ell$ with initial flag $b$ is a sublist of $\ell$: it is obtained from $\ell$ by deleting some elements and keeping the rest in order.

results.title: The sample is a sublist
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $\ell$, the sample of $\ell$ is a sublist of $\ell$: it is obtained from $\ell$ by deleting some elements and keeping the rest in order.

results.title: Entries of a sample are entries of the catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a catalog (finite list) $L$, every entry of the sample of $L$ (every other entry of $L$, starting with the first) is an entry of $L$.

results.title: Doubled sample length bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every catalog $L$, twice the length of the sample of $L$ is at most the length of $L$ plus one.

results.title: The sample has at most half the length, rounded up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ (over any type), the sample of $xs$ has length at most $\lfloor (|xs| + 1)/2 \rfloor$, half the length of $xs$ rounded up: for an even length $2m$ the bound is $m$, and for an odd length $2m + 1$ it is $m + 1$.

results.title: The sample is no longer than the list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ (over any type), the sample of $xs$, every other element starting with the first, has length at most the length of $xs$.

results.title: The sample of a sorted list is sorted
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a list over a linear order is sorted in nondecreasing order, then so is its sample.

results.title: Sorted merge of two catalogs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linearly ordered type, their sorted merge is the result of merge sort, with respect to $\le$, applied to the concatenation of $\ell_1$ followed by $\ell_2$.

results.title: A sorted merge rearranges the concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order, the sorted merge of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ is a permutation of the concatenation of $\ell_1$ followed by $\ell_2$.

results.title: Length of a sorted merge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For catalogs (finite lists) $L$ and $M$ over a linearly ordered type, the sorted merge of $L$ and $M$ has length equal to the length of $L$ plus the length of $M$.

results.title: A sorted merge is sorted
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order, sorted or not, their sorted merge is sorted in nondecreasing order.

results.title: Elements of a sorted merge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order and any element $v$, $v$ belongs to the sorted merge of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ if and only if $v$ belongs to $\ell_1$ or to $\ell_2$.

results.title: Lower bound of a value in a catalog
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a value $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a catalog (finite list) $L$, the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ is the number of entries of $L$ that are less than $x$, counted with multiplicity. For a sorted catalog this is the first index whose entry is not less than $x$, or the length of $L$ if there is none.

results.title: Lower bound is at most the catalog length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ (the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$) is at most the length of $L$.

results.title: Lower bound in a sorted merge splits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$ and catalogs $L$ and $M$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the sorted merge of $L$ and $M$ equals the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ plus the lower bound of $x$ in $M$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of its entries less than $x$.

results.title: Lower bound in a sample is at most the lower bound in the catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the number of entries less than $x$ in the sample of $L$ (every other entry of $L$, starting with the first) is at most the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$.

results.title: Scan count of smaller elements
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$, the scan count of $x$ in $L$ is the number of elements of $L$ that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan: it is $0$ for the empty catalog, and for a catalog with head $a$ and tail $L'$ it is the scan count of $x$ in $L'$, plus $1$ if $a < x$.

results.title: The scan count equals the lower bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every value $x$ and every catalog $L$, the scan count of elements of $L$ that are $< x$ equals the lower bound of $x$ in $L$.

results.title: Augmenting a catalog by the next one
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For catalogs $c$ and $a$, the augmentation of $c$ by $a$ is the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$ (every other element of $a$, starting with the first). In fractional cascading, $a$ is the next augmented catalog.

results.title: One augmentation step yields a sorted list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any lists $c$ and $a$ over a linear order, sorted or not, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample of $a$ is sorted in nondecreasing order.

results.title: Length of one augmented catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample $s(a)$ of $a$ has length $|c| + |s(a)|$.

results.title: Length bound for one augmented catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample of $a$ has length at most $|c| + \lfloor (|a| + 1)/2 \rfloor$, the length of $c$ plus half the length of $a$ rounded up.

results.title: Membership in an augmented catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, a value $v$ is an entry of the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) if and only if $v$ is an entry of $c$ or an entry of the sample of $a$.

results.title: Entries of an augmented catalog come from the two catalogs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, every entry $v$ of the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) is an entry of $c$ or an entry of $a$.

results.title: Lower bound in an augmented catalog splits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$ and catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) equals the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ plus the lower bound of $x$ in the sample of $a$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of its entries less than $x$.

results.title: Lower bound in an augmented catalog is at most the sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$ and catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) is at most the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ plus the lower bound of $x$ in $a$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of its entries less than $x$.

results.title: Augmenting a catalog by the head of a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a catalog $c$ and a list $L$ of catalogs, the result is $c$ itself if $L$ is empty, and otherwise the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample (every other element, starting with the first) of the first catalog of $L$.

results.title: Augmented catalogs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of catalogs $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the augmented catalogs $A_1, \dots, A_k$ are built from the last one backwards: $A_k = c_k$, and for $i < k$, $A_i$ is the sorted merge of $c_i$ with the sample (every other element, starting with the first) of $A_{i+1}$. The empty list of catalogs has no augmented catalogs.

results.title: Number of augmented catalogs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $cs$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, the list of augmented catalogs built from $cs$ has the same length as $cs$: there is one augmented catalog per catalog.

results.title: Augmenting a single catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every catalog $c$, the list of augmented catalogs of the one-element list $[c]$ is $[c]$: the only augmented catalog is $c$ itself.

results.title: The augmented catalogs of sorted catalogs are sorted
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If every catalog in a list of catalogs over a linear order is sorted in nondecreasing order, then every augmented catalog built from that list is sorted in nondecreasing order.

results.title: Augmented catalogs are bounded by the total input size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $cs = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, every augmented catalog built from $cs$ has length at most $|c_1| + \dots + |c_k|$.

results.title: Bridge pointer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a catalog $L$ and a value $v$, the bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$ is the number of elements of $L$ that are $\le v$.

results.title: Bridge pointers are at most the catalog length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every catalog $L$ and value $v$, the bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$ is at most the length of $L$.

results.title: Bridge pointer list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For catalogs $C$ and $L$, the bridge pointers of $C$ into $L$ form the list obtained by replacing each entry $v$ of $C$, in order, by the bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$.

results.title: Number of bridge pointers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists $c$ and $d$ over a linearly ordered type, the list of bridge pointers of $c$ into $d$ has the same length as $c$: there is one bridge pointer per entry of $c$.

results.title: Bridge pointers are at most the next catalog's length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists $c$ and $d$ over a linearly ordered type, every entry $p$ of the list of bridge pointers of $c$ into $d$ satisfies $p \le |d|$, where $|d|$ is the length of $d$; so every recorded bridge pointer is a boundary index of $d$.

results.title: Searching every catalog
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs, the search returns, for each catalog in order, the number of its elements that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan of that catalog. This is the lower-bound position of $x$ in each catalog.

results.title: Searching no catalogs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Searching the empty list of catalogs for any value $x$ gives the empty list of positions.

results.title: Searching a nonempty list of catalogs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$, a catalog $c$ and a list of catalogs $cs$, searching $c$ followed by $cs$ for $x$ gives first the direct-scan count of the elements of $c$ that are $< x$, followed by the positions obtained by searching $cs$ for $x$.

results.title: One search position per catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every value $x$ and every list $cs$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, searching each catalog of $cs$ for $x$ gives a list of positions of the same length as $cs$.

results.title: Correctness of searching every catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs $c_1, \dots, c_k$, searching every catalog for $x$ returns the list whose $i$-th entry is the lower bound of $x$ in $c_i$, that is, the number of elements of $c_i$ that are $< x$.

results.title: Search positions are lower bounds, index by index
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every value $x$, list of catalogs $C_0, \dots, C_{k-1}$ and index $i$: if $i < k$, the $i$-th position returned by searching all catalogs for $x$ is the lower bound of $x$ in $C_i$; if $i \ge k$, the search result has no $i$-th entry.

results.title: Search positions are boundary indices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a value and let $cs$ be a list of catalogs whose entry at index $i$ is the catalog $c$. Then searching every catalog of $cs$ for $x$ gives, at index $i$, the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ (the number of elements of $c$ that are $< x$), and this lower bound is at most the length of $c$.

results.title: Searching every augmented catalog
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs, the augmented search builds the augmented catalogs and returns, for each augmented catalog in order, the number of its elements that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan of that catalog.

results.title: One augmented search position per catalog
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every value $x$ and every list $cs$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, searching each augmented catalog built from $cs$ for $x$ gives a list of positions of the same length as $cs$.

results.title: Correctness of augmented search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs $cs$, searching every augmented catalog of $cs$ for $x$ returns, for each augmented catalog in order, the lower bound of $x$ in it, that is, the number of its elements that are $< x$.

results.title: Being the maximum subarray sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $L$ over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, an element $m \in \alpha$ is the maximum subarray sum of $L$ when some nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum $m$ and every nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum at most $m$.

results.title: Being the maximum suffix sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $L$ over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, an element $e \in \alpha$ is the maximum suffix sum of $L$ when some nonempty suffix of $L$ has sum $e$ and every nonempty suffix of $L$ has sum at most $e$. A nonempty suffix is a contiguous run ending at the last element of $L$.

results.title: Kadane's scan
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given accumulators $e, b$ in an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, the scan over the empty list returns $b$ at cost $0$. Over a list with first element $x$ and remaining elements $L$, it sets $e' = \max(x, e + x)$ and returns the result of the scan of $L$ from the accumulators $e'$ and $\max(b, e')$, at cost $3$ plus the cost of that scan.

results.title: Kadane's algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type with an additive monoid structure. On the empty list, Kadane's algorithm returns no value. On a list $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ of elements of $\alpha$ with $n \ge 1$, it sets $e = b = x_1$; then for $i = 2, \dots, n$ in turn it replaces $e$ by $\max(x_i, e + x_i)$ and then $b$ by $\max(b, e)$; finally it returns $b$. Each of the steps $i = 2, \dots, n$ is charged three…

results.title: Cost of Kadane's scan
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. For all accumulators $e, b \in \alpha$ and every list $L$ over $\alpha$ of length $n$, Kadane's scan of $L$ from the accumulators $e$ and $b$ costs exactly $3n$.

results.title: Cost of Kadane's algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, Kadane's algorithm on a list of length $n \ge 1$ costs exactly $3(n - 1)$ operations, and on the empty list it costs $0$.

results.title: A list with a maximum subarray sum is nonempty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. If an element $m \in \alpha$ is the maximum subarray sum of a list $L$ over $\alpha$, then $L$ is nonempty.

results.title: Uniqueness of the maximum subarray sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type with an additive monoid structure, and let $L$ be a list over $\alpha$. If $m, m' \in \alpha$ are both maximum subarray sums of $L$, meaning that each is the sum of some nonempty contiguous run of $L$ and bounds the sum of every nonempty contiguous run of $L$, then $m = m'$.

results.title: Maximum suffix sum after appending an element
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. If $e$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix of a list $p$ over $\alpha$, then for every $x \in \alpha$ the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix of the list obtained by appending $x$ to $p$ is $\max(x, e + x)$.

results.title: Maximum subarray sum after appending an element
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. Let $p$ be a list over $\alpha$, let $e$ be the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix of $p$, and let $b$ be the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous sublist of $p$. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous sublist of the list obtained by appending $x$ to $p$ is $\max(b, \max(x, e + x))$.

results.title: Invariant of Kadane's scan
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. Let $p$ be a list over $\alpha$, let $e$ be the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix of $p$, and let $b$ be the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous sublist of $p$. Then for every list $r$ over $\alpha$, the value that Kadane's scan from the accumulators $e$ and $b$ returns on $r$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty…

results.title: Correctness of Kadane's algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. For every list $L$ over $\alpha$ and every $m \in \alpha$, Kadane's algorithm returns $m$ on $L$ if and only if $m$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$: some nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum $m$, and every nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum at most $m$.

results.title: Kadane's algorithm bounds every nonempty run
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type with an additive monoid structure in which $b \le c$ implies $b + a \le c + a$. If Kadane's algorithm returns the value $m$ on a list $L$ over $\alpha$, then every nonempty contiguous run of $L$ has sum at most $m$.

results.title: Kadane's algorithm returns an attained sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. If Kadane's algorithm returns a value $m$ on a list $L$ over $\alpha$, then some nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum $m$.

results.title: Maximum prefix sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. For a list $xs$ over $\alpha$ and $p \in \alpha$, $p$ is the maximum prefix sum of $xs$ when some nonempty prefix of $xs$ has sum $p$ and every nonempty prefix of $xs$ has sum at most $p$.

results.title: Right-to-left suffix scan
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid carrying a linear order. For a nonempty list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ in $\alpha$, this timed computation returns the pair $(x_1 + \dots + x_n, s)$, where $s$ is the maximum of the suffix sums $x_i + \dots + x_n$ over $1 \le i \le n$. It scans from the right: the step for $x_i$ forms $x_i + (x_{i+1} + \dots + x_n)$ and takes its maximum with the best suffix sum found so far, at a cost of…

results.title: Prefix scan
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For lists over an additive monoid with a linear order, the prefix scan returns $0$ on the empty list at no cost, and $x$ on a one-element list $[x]$ at cost $2$. On a list with first element $x$ and nonempty tail $t$ it returns $\max(x, x + b)$, where $b$ is the prefix scan of $t$, at the cost of the scan of $t$ plus $2$.

results.title: Divide-and-conquer core of maximum subarray
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For lists over an additive monoid with a linear order: on the empty list it returns $0$ and on a one-element list $[x]$ it returns $x$, both at no cost. On a list of length $n \ge 2$, let $m = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $l$ and $r$ be its results on the first $m$ elements and on the remaining $n - m$ elements, let $s$ be the best nonempty suffix sum of the first $m$ elements as computed by the suffix scan, and let…

results.title: Divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The CLRS algorithm FIND-MAXIMUM-SUBARRAY over an additive monoid with a linear order, returning only the sum. On the empty list it returns no value, at no cost. On a nonempty list it returns the value of the divide-and-conquer core on that list, at the same cost; the core splits a list of length $n \ge 2$ after its first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ elements and returns the largest of its results on the two parts and the…

results.title: Cost recurrence of divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The function $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ given by $T(n) = 0$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = T(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + T(n - \lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + 2n + 3$ for $n \ge 2$.

results.title: Running time of divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. On a nonempty list over $\alpha$ of length $n$, the cost $T$ of the divide-and-conquer maximum subarray algorithm satisfies $T + 3 \le 2n\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 3n$, that is, $T \le 2n\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 3(n - 1)$.

results.title: Correctness of the suffix scan
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. For every nonempty list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the suffix scan of $xs$ returns a pair whose first component is the sum of $xs$ and whose second component is the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix of $xs$.

results.title: Maximum subarray sum of a concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $b \le c$ implies $a + b \le a + c$ and $b + a \le c + a$, and let $L$ and $R$ be lists over $\alpha$. Suppose that $l$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of $L$, $r$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of $R$, $s$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix of $L$, and $p$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty prefix of $R$. Then…

results.title: Correctness of divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $b \le c$ implies $a + b \le a + c$ and $b + a \le c + a$. For every list $xs$ over $\alpha$ and every $m \in \alpha$, the divide-and-conquer algorithm returns $m$ on $xs$ if and only if $m$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of $xs$.

results.title: Divide and conquer agrees with Kadane's algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such that $b \le c$ implies $a + b \le a + c$ and $b + a \le c + a$. For every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the divide-and-conquer maximum subarray algorithm and Kadane's algorithm return the same result on $xs$.

results.title: Min-hash of a set under a permutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The min-hash of `A` under the permutation `π`: the least element of `π(A)`, or `⊤` if `A` is empty.

results.title: MinHash, counting form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The number of permutations of `U` under which `A` and `B` have the same min-hash, times `|A ∪ B|`, equals `|A ∩ B|` times the number of all permutations.

results.title: MinHash collision probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: MinHash collision probability (Broder 1997): for a uniformly random permutation `π` of the finite universe `U` (`uniformOn Set.univ` on `Equiv.Perm U`, for any measurable structure in which singletons are measurable, e.g. `⊤`) and sets `A`, `B` with `A ∪ B` nonempty, `P(min π(A) = min π(B)) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|`, the Jaccard similarity of `A` and `B`.

results.title: Channel names of go-back-N
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The channel names of the go-back-N protocol are $\mathsf{acc}$ (accept a message from the user), $\mathsf{del}$ (deliver a message to the user) and, for every natural number $k$: $\mathsf{send}\,k$ (sender to data channel, a frame with sequence number $k$), $\mathsf{recv}\,k$ (data channel to receiver), $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ (receiver to sender, the cumulative acknowledgement naming $k$ as the next expected frame) and…

results.title: Go-back-N sender state
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A state of the go-back-N sender is a triple of natural numbers: the base of the window (the sequence number of the oldest unacknowledged frame), the number of outstanding messages (accepted but not yet acknowledged), and the offset from the base of the next frame to transmit.

results.title: Receiver states of go-back-N
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A receiver state is one of the following, for a natural number $e$ or $k$: expecting the frame with sequence number $e$; about to deliver $e$, having received the expected frame $e$; or about to acknowledge $k$, the next expected sequence number.

results.title: Sender update on an acknowledgement
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a go-back-N sender with window base $b$, $c$ outstanding messages and next-frame offset $o$, and an acknowledgement $k$, let $d = \max(k + 3 - b, 0) \bmod 3$. If $1 \le d \le c$, the window slides: the new sender has base $k$, $c - d$ outstanding messages and next-frame offset $\max(o - d, 0)$. Otherwise the sender is unchanged.

results.title: Sender transitions of go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transitions of a sender with window base $b$, $n$ outstanding messages and next offset $o$, as pairs of a label and a successor state, in this order: if $n < 2$, an input on $\mathsf{acc}$ to $(b, n + 1, o)$; if $o < n$, an output on $\mathsf{send}\,((b + o) \bmod 3)$ to $(b, n, o + 1)$; if $0 < n$, a silent timeout step to $(b, n, 0)$; and, for each $k = 0, 1, 2$, an input on $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ to the state…

results.title: Transitions of the go-back-N data channel
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The data channel holds at most one frame. When empty, for each sequence number $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ it can input on channel $\mathrm{send}_k$ and then hold frame $k$. When holding frame $k$, it can either output on channel $\mathrm{recv}_k$ or silently lose the frame by a $\tau$ step; in both cases it becomes empty.

results.title: Receiver transitions of go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transitions of the receiver, as pairs of a label and a successor state. Expecting $e$, for each $k = 0, 1, 2$ it can input on $\mathsf{recv}\,k$ and then is about to deliver $e$ if $k = e$, and about to acknowledge $e$ otherwise. About to deliver $e$, it outputs on $\mathsf{del}$ and is then about to acknowledge $(e + 1) \bmod 3$. About to acknowledge $k$, it outputs on $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ and then expects $k$.

results.title: Transitions of the two-place buffer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transitions of the go-back-N two-place buffer at occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$: if $n < 2$ it inputs on $\mathsf{acc}$ and moves to occupancy $n + 1$, and if $n > 0$ it outputs on $\mathsf{del}$ and moves to occupancy $n - 1$. It has no other transitions.

results.title: Transitions of the lossy acknowledgement channel
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The lossy one-place acknowledgement channel of the lossy go-back-N variant, given by its transitions in each state. When empty, it inputs on $\mathsf{reply}_k$ and then holds $k$, for each $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. When it holds $k$, it either outputs on $\mathsf{ack}_k$ or silently loses $k$, and in both cases it becomes empty. It has no other transitions.

results.title: Receiver transitions of lossy go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transitions of the receiver of the lossy variant, as pairs of a label and a successor state, are those of the receiver of the reliable protocol, except in the state about to acknowledge $k$: there the only transition is an output on $\mathsf{reply}\,k$, to the acknowledgement channel, after which the receiver expects $k$.

results.title: Process constants of the go-back-N model
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The process constants of the go-back-N specification, one for each state of each component: a sender constant for each sender state, a data-channel constant for each channel content (empty or a natural number), a receiver constant for each receiver state, a buffer constant for each occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$, an acknowledgement-channel constant for each channel content (empty or a natural number), and a constant…

results.title: Recursive CCS specification of go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The specification assigns to every process constant the choice, over the transitions listed for its state, of the prefixes $a.K$, where $a$ is the label of the transition and $K$ is the process constant for its target state; an empty list gives the inactive process. The constants are those of the sender, the data channel, the receiver, the two-place buffer, the acknowledgement channel and the receiver of the lossy…

results.title: Labelled transition system of go-back-N
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The labelled transition system whose states are the CCS processes over the go-back-N channel names and process constants, whose labels are the CCS labels over the channel names, and whose transitions are those generated by the go-back-N recursive specification.

results.title: Internal channels of go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The internal channels of the go-back-N protocol are $\mathrm{send}_k$ (sender to data channel), $\mathrm{recv}_k$ (data channel to receiver) and $\mathrm{ack}_k$ (receiver to sender) for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$; all of them are restricted.

results.title: Go-back-N configurations
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A configuration of the go-back-N protocol consists of a sender state, the content of the data channel (either empty or a single frame with sequence number $k \in \mathbb{N}$), and a receiver state.

results.title: Go-back-N protocol process in a configuration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a configuration consisting of a sender state $s$, a data channel content $d$ (empty or one frame) and a receiver state $r$, the protocol process is the parallel composition $(S_s \mid D_d) \mid R_r$ of the process constants for the sender in state $s$, the data channel holding $d$ and the receiver in state $r$, with the internal channels restricted: the send, receive and acknowledgement channels for the…

results.title: Transitions of go-back-N configurations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transitions of a go-back-N configuration (sender, data channel, receiver) are those of the parallel composition of the three components, in which one component moves alone or two components synchronize on complementary labels in a silent step, restricted to the silent steps and the steps whose label is not on an internal channel ($\mathsf{send}_k$, $\mathsf{recv}_k$ or $\mathsf{ack}_k$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$).

results.title: The two-place buffer process
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process constant of the go-back-N specification for the two-place buffer holding $n$ messages.

results.title: Initial configuration of go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The initial configuration of the go-back-N protocol consists of the sender with window base $0$, no outstanding messages and next-frame offset $0$; the empty data channel; and the receiver expecting sequence number $0$.

results.title: The go-back-N protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The go-back-N protocol with window size $2$ and sequence numbers modulo $3$ is the recursive CCS process in its initial configuration: the parallel composition of the sender with an empty window based at $0$, the empty lossy one-place data channel, and the receiver expecting $0$, with the internal channels $\mathrm{send}_k$, $\mathrm{recv}_k$ and $\mathrm{ack}_k$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ restricted.

results.title: The empty two-place buffer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The two-place buffer process of the go-back-N model with occupancy $0$.

results.title: Weak-bisimulation certificate for go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A list of $147$ pairs, each a go-back-N configuration together with the occupancy of the two-place buffer it simulates, namely the number of accepted but undelivered messages. It contains every reachable configuration, and it is ordered so that every pair can reach the visible actions of its buffer state through pairs listed earlier.

results.title: Go-back-N with window 2 implements a two-place buffer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Over a lossy one-place data channel, with timeouts and cumulative acknowledgements, the protocol is weakly bisimilar to the empty two-place buffer.

results.title: Go-back-N with window 2 is observation congruent to a two-place buffer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The go-back-N protocol is observation congruent (rooted weakly bisimilar) to the empty two-place buffer: every transition of either process is matched by a rooted weak transition of the other with the same label (silent steps, a step with that label, silent steps), and the resulting processes are weakly bisimilar.

results.title: Internal channels of lossy go-back-N
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The list of channels restricted in the lossy variant: the internal channels of the reliable protocol, namely $\mathsf{send}\,k$, $\mathsf{recv}\,k$ and $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$, followed by the channels $\mathsf{reply}\,0$, $\mathsf{reply}\,1$ and $\mathsf{reply}\,2$ from the receiver to the acknowledgement channel.

results.title: Configurations of lossy go-back-N
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A configuration of the lossy go-back-N variant is a go-back-N configuration (sender state, data channel content, receiver state) together with the content of the acknowledgement channel, either empty or a single acknowledgement $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: The lossy go-back-N process in a configuration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $c$ be a configuration of the lossy variant, and let $S$, $D$, $R$ and $A$ be the process constants for its sender state, its data-channel content, its receiver state (as a receiver of the lossy variant) and its acknowledgement-channel content. The process of the lossy variant in $c$ is $((S \mid D) \mid R) \mid A$ with the internal channels of the lossy variant restricted.

results.title: Transitions of lossy go-back-N configurations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transitions of a configuration of the lossy go-back-N variant come from the parallel composition of the sender, the data channel, the lossy-variant receiver and the acknowledgement channel (in each composition either side moves alone, or the two sides synchronize on complementary input and output labels in a silent step), keeping only the silent transitions and those whose label is not on an internal channel…

results.title: Go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The process of the lossy variant of go-back-N in its initial configuration: the sender's window is based at $0$ with no outstanding messages and next offset $0$, the data channel and the acknowledgement channel are empty, and the receiver expects frame $0$.

results.title: Configuration transitions are process transitions in lossy go-back-N
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ and $c'$ be configurations of the lossy variant and $a$ a label. If $(a, c')$ is one of the configuration-level transitions of $c$, then in the labelled transition system of the go-back-N specification the lossy process in configuration $c$ has a transition labelled $a$ to the lossy process in configuration $c'$.

results.title: The silent closure of the buffer is trivial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every occupancy $n$, every process reachable from the go-back-N buffer with occupancy $n$ by zero or more silent steps is that buffer itself.

results.title: Visible weak steps of the buffer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every occupancy $n$ and every visible label $a$, if the go-back-N buffer with occupancy $n$ reaches a process $Q$ by a weak transition labelled $a$ (silent steps, one $a$-step, silent steps), then $Q$ is the buffer with some occupancy $m$ such that the buffer at occupancy $n$ has a transition labelled $a$ to occupancy $m$.

results.title: Silent closure of the stuck lossy go-back-N configuration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The list of the seven configurations of go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel in which the sender's window has base $0$ with two outstanding messages, the receiver holds frame $1$ about to deliver it, and the acknowledgement channel is empty, while the sender's offset of the next frame to transmit and the data channel are, in order: offset $2$ and empty, offset $0$ and empty, offset $1$ holding frame $0$,…

results.title: The stuck lossy go-back-N configuration refuses new messages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Consider go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel in the configuration where the sender's window has base $0$ with two outstanding messages, both transmitted (offset of the next frame $2$), the data channel and the acknowledgement channel are empty, and the receiver holds frame $1$ about to deliver it. This process has no weak transition labelled by accepting a message: no sequence of silent steps followed by…

results.title: Lossy acknowledgements break the buffer specification
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With a lossy acknowledgement channel and the deliver-then-acknowledge receiver, go-back-N is not weakly bisimilar to the two-place buffer. Accept two messages, deliver the first and lose its acknowledgement, and let the receiver take the second frame: the buffer now holds one message and accepts another, but the protocol cannot accept before it delivers.
